## Background

The data set consists of about 10'000 peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from one 10x Genomics run.
Each cell carries a `cellType` label that was derived with additional data and serves as ground truth here.
There are 29 cell types. A cell is `unassigned` if no cell type could be assigned reliably.

You will do two things that every single-cell analysis starts with: remove low-quality cells and cluster the rest.
Because the ground truth is known, you can check what these two steps really do.

**Learning goals.** After this exercise you can

1. compute per-cell quality metrics and judge what a quality filter removes;
2. compare a clustering with known cell types, with a contingency table and with a single number;
3. explain, with examples from this data set, why clusters and cell types do not match one to one;
4. tell a harmless mismatch (one cell type in several clusters) from a harmful one (several cell types in one cluster).

**How to work.** Several tasks start with *Predict*. Write your prediction down *before* you run the code.
A wrong prediction is not a mistake; the comparison with the result is the point of the task.


**What to hand in.** Start from this Quarto file and add your answers and code. Hand in the quarto and the rendered html.

The workflow is inspired by <http://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA/>.


The full data set gives the clearest picture. If your computer is slow, reduce `nCells`; rare cell types then get very small.

```{r subsample cells}
nCells = 5000
set.seed(38)
if (ncol(sce) > nCells) {
  sce = sce[ , sample(ncol(sce), size = nCells, replace = FALSE)]
}
```

The annotation is fine-grained. The table below groups the labels into major cell types; you will need both levels.

```{r major cell types}
majorMap = c(
```

## Part 1: Quality control

### 1.1 Quality metrics

```{r quality scores}
isMito = grepl("^MT-", rowData(sce)$Symbol)
sce = addPerCellQC(sce, subsets = list(Mito = isMito))
colnames(colData(sce))
```

### 1.2 A standard filter

`perCellQCFilters()` flags cells that lie more than 3 median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median: too few UMIs, too few genes,
or too high a mitochondrial percentage.

**Task** *Guess before running the chunk:* which share of the `unassigned` cells will this filter remove?
Will it remove cells of any assigned cell type?

```{r standard filter}
qc = perCellQCFilters(sce, sub.fields = "subsets_Mito_percent")
colSums(as.matrix(qc))
sce$discard = qc$discard
```

```{r filter by cell type}
qcByType = data.frame(
  nCells = as.vector(table(sce$cellType)),
  discarded = as.vector(tapply(sce$discard, sce$cellType, sum)),
  row.names = names(table(sce$cellType)))
qcByType$fraction = round(qcByType$discarded / qcByType$nCells, 2)
qcByType[order(-qcByType$fraction), ]
```

The original idea of this exercise was to treat `unassigned` as "low quality". The two numbers below measure the filter in that sense.

```{r sensitivity}
isUnassigned = sce$cellType == "unassigned"
c(sensitivity = mean(sce$discard[isUnassigned]),      # unassigned cells that are removed
  specificity = mean(!sce$discard[!isUnassigned]))    # assigned cells that are kept
```

**Task** Compare with your prediction.

a) Is "unassigned" the same as "low quality"? Use the metric plots of the unassigned cells that the filter keeps.
b) Which assigned cell types does the filter remove almost completely? Are these low-quality cells?

## Part 2: Clustering against the ground truth

### 2.1 Normalization, feature selection, PCA

```{r preprocess}
preprocess = function(sce, nHvg = 2000, nPcs = 30) {
  sce = sce[Matrix::rowSums(counts(sce) > 0) >= 5, ]
  sce = logNormCounts(sce)
  dec = modelGeneVarByPoisson(sce)
  hvg = getTopHVGs(dec, n = nHvg)
  set.seed(38)
  sce = runPCA(sce, subset_row = hvg, ncomponents = nPcs)
  sce = runUMAP(sce, dimred = "PCA")
  sce
}
sceFilt = preprocess(sceFilt)
```

```{r umap truth, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
plotReducedDim(sceFilt, "UMAP", colour_by = "majorType")
plotReducedDim(sceFilt, "UMAP", colour_by = "cellType", text_by = "cellType", text_size = 3) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Task** Look at the two plots. Which cell types form separate islands, and which ones overlap within an island?


### 2.2 Two kinds of mismatch, and tools to measure them

A clustering can disagree with the cell types in two ways, and they are not equally bad.

- **Split:** one cell type is spread over several clusters. This is a minor nuisance. If every one of these clusters contains only
  that cell type, you give them the same label and merge them. Nothing is lost.
- **Mixed:** one cluster contains several cell types. This is the real problem. No label can repair it: whatever name the cluster
  gets, the cells of the other types are wrong, and every downstream comparison treats them as one population.

The helper functions below measure both. Read them and make sure you understand what they compute.

```{r helper functions}
## label every cluster with its most frequent cell type ("majority label")
majorityLabel = function(cluster, cellType) {
  tab = unclass(table(cluster, cellType))
  lab = colnames(tab)[apply(tab, 1, which.max)]
  names(lab) = rownames(tab)
  unname(lab[as.character(cluster)])
}

## summary of one clustering
##   ari        adjusted Rand index of the raw clusters: punishes split AND mixed
##   purity     share of cells whose cluster's majority label is their own cell type: punishes only mixed
##   ariMerged  ARI after merging clusters with the same majority label: what is left after repairing the splits
evalClustering = function(cluster, cellType) {
  use = cellType != "unassigned"
  cluster = as.character(cluster[use]); cellType = cellType[use]
  merged = majorityLabel(cluster, cellType)
  c(nClusters = length(unique(cluster)),
    ari = mclust::adjustedRandIndex(cluster, cellType),
    purity = mean(merged == cellType),
    ariMerged = mclust::adjustedRandIndex(merged, cellType))
}

## per cell type
##   nClust         number of clusters that hold at least 10 % of the cell type (split)
##   inOwnClusters  share of the cell type that sits in clusters where it is the majority (not mixed away)
matchTable = function(cluster, cellType) {
  tab = unclass(table(cellType, cluster))
  merged = majorityLabel(cluster, cellType)
  data.frame(cellType = rownames(tab), nCells = rowSums(tab),
             nClust = rowSums(tab / rowSums(tab) >= 0.1),
             inOwnClusters = round(as.vector(tapply(merged == cellType, cellType, mean)[rownames(tab)]), 2),
             row.names = NULL)
}
```

A cell type is *recovered* if most of its cells (say, at least 70 %) sit in clusters where it is the majority. It may be split over
several such clusters.

**Task** `purity` can only be computed with a ground truth. Which value does it take if every cell is its own cluster?
What does that tell you about using purity alone to choose a clustering?

### 2.3 A first clustering

```{r kmeans}
set.seed(100)
sceFilt$kmeans10 = factor(kmeans(reducedDim(sceFilt, "PCA"), centers = 10)$cluster)
round(evalClustering(sceFilt$kmeans10, sceFilt$cellType), 2)
```

```{r kmeans heatmap, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
tab = unclass(table(sceFilt$cellType, sceFilt$kmeans10))
pheatmap(tab / rowSums(tab), cluster_cols = FALSE,
         main = "share of each cell type (row) per cluster (column)")
mt = matchTable(sceFilt$kmeans10, sceFilt$cellType)
mt[order(-mt$nCells), ]
```


### 2.4 Resolution: splitting is cheap, mixing is not

Graph-based clustering is the standard for single-cell data. The resolution parameter controls the number of clusters.

```{r graph clustering}
clusterGraph = function(sce, k = 15, resolution = 1) {
  clusterCells(sce, use.dimred = "PCA",
               BLUSPARAM = NNGraphParam(k = k, cluster.fun = "louvain",
                                        cluster.args = list(resolution = resolution)))
}
set.seed(100)
sceFilt$graph1 = clusterGraph(sceFilt, resolution = 1)
round(evalClustering(sceFilt$graph1, sceFilt$cellType), 2)
```
